sw_001:n1.prompt:
You are helping me complete the "Write the spec" step for a new feature we're shipping, using {{vendor}} (our project-management tool) as the system of record.

Before starting, ask me for: (1) the feature name and a one-paragraph description of what it should do and why, (2) which {{vendor}} workspace/project or database this spec should live in, and (3) any existing docs, tickets, or prior specs you should reference for context or format consistency.

Once you have that, do the following:
1. Using my configured credentials for {{vendor}}, create a new page (or doc) for this feature spec inside the workspace/project I specified.
2. Structure the spec with clear sections: Problem/Goal, Proposed Solution, Scope (in/out), User Stories or Acceptance Criteria, Open Questions, and Risks/Dependencies.
3. If {{vendor}} has a built-in AI assistant, use it to help draft or refine sections of the spec text, then write/update the page's content blocks with the final draft.
4. Cross-link or reference any related docs/notes already in {{vendor}} so the spec sits alongside relevant project work, per the tool's shared-docs organization features.
5. Leave clearly marked placeholders or bracketed notes for any information you don't have (e.g., exact metrics, deadlines) rather than guessing.

Done looks like: a complete, well-organized spec page live in {{vendor}}, with all sections filled in or explicitly flagged as needing my input, ready for me to review before it moves into tracking/implementation.

Report back with: the page title, its location (project/workspace) in {{vendor}}, a link if available, a short summary of what you wrote, and a list of any open questions or missing inputs you flagged for me.

sw_001:n2.prompt:
You are helping me ship a feature from spec to deploy. This step: create the tracking issue for the feature in {{vendor}}, my project-management tool, so the work has one place to live through implementation, review, and deploy.

Ask me for anything missing before you start:
- The feature spec, or a link to it. A previous step should have produced it.
- The {{vendor}} workspace and team or project where the issue belongs.
- The assignee, if not me.
- A due date, if any.
- Priority and labels I use (for example "feature").
- Whether my code repository's issue tracker is synced with {{vendor}}.

Actions:
1. Use your configured credentials to connect to {{vendor}} through its documented public API. Fall back to the web app only if the API is unavailable.
2. First, search the target team or project for an existing issue covering this feature. If one exists, show it to me and ask whether to reuse it instead of creating a duplicate.
3. Create one issue with:
   - A short, action-oriented title.
   - A description holding a one-paragraph summary, the acceptance criteria as a checklist, out-of-scope notes, and a link to the full spec.
   - The assignee, due date, priority, and labels I confirmed.
4. If repository sync is enabled, confirm the issue appears on the repository side rather than creating it twice. If sync is not enabled, do not create a separate repository issue unless I ask.
5. Read the issue back from {{vendor}} to confirm every field saved correctly.

Done looks like this: exactly one tracking issue exists in {{vendor}}, it is correctly assigned, and its fields match what I confirmed.

Report back with:
- The issue's identifier and URL.
- The title, assignee, due date, priority, and labels.
- The sync status with my repository.
- A suggested branch name derived from the issue identifier, for the coding agent to use in the next step.

If anything failed or was ambiguous, say so plainly. Do not guess.

sw_001:n3.prompt:
You are helping me implement a specific feature or bug fix using {{vendor}}, our AI coding agent tool, as part of shipping a tracked issue from spec to deploy. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) the tracked issue or spec (ticket link, description, or acceptance criteria), (2) the repository name/path and branch to work from, and (3) whether this should run locally or as a background cloud task in {{vendor}}.

Once you have the spec and repo, use {{vendor}} to: turn the issue into a working implementation across all necessary files; write or update tests covering the new behavior; run the test suite and fix any failures; resolve lint errors; update dependencies if the change requires it; and resolve any merge conflicts against the target branch. If the task is long-running, delegate it to run in {{vendor}}'s isolated cloud environment rather than blocking locally. Where possible, drive this programmatically via the Agent.create(...) SDK call so the run is reproducible and logged.

As you work, narrow down root cause if this is a bug fix, and verify the fix actually resolves the reported issue (not just that tests pass). Keep a running log of: files changed, tests added/modified, lint/dependency fixes applied, and any conflicts resolved.

Done looks like: a complete, locally verified (tests passing, lint clean) code change on a branch, ready to be opened as a pull request in the next step. Report back with a summary of the implementation approach, the branch name, list of changed files, test results, and any open questions or risks I should know about before the PR is opened.

sw_001:n4.prompt:
You are helping me open a pull request on {{vendor}} for a feature branch I've just finished implementing. If you don't already know them, ask me for: the {{vendor}} repository (owner/name), the feature branch name, the base branch to merge into (e.g. main or develop), and the related spec/ticket reference (issue number or link) that describes what this feature does.

Using your configured credentials, please:
1. Confirm the feature branch exists on the remote and has commits ahead of the base branch.
2. Create a pull/merge request on {{vendor}} from the feature branch into the base branch.
3. Write a clear PR title summarizing the change, and a description that includes: a summary of what changed and why, a link or reference to the originating spec/ticket, a checklist of testing done (or to be done), and any notes for reviewers (e.g. areas needing extra scrutiny, breaking changes, migration steps).
4. Set the PR to draft mode if the implementation is not fully ready for review, or ready-for-review otherwise — ask me which if unclear.
5. Add any requested reviewers or labels if I specify them; otherwise leave defaults.
6. Enable the option for reviewers to respond with inline comments if the platform requires explicit configuration.

Done looks like: a pull/merge request exists on {{vendor}} with a populated title, description, correct base/head branches, and appropriate draft/ready status — ready for AI and human review to begin.

Report back with: the PR URL, its current status (draft/ready), the title and a short summary of the description you wrote, and any reviewers/labels applied. Flag anything ambiguous (e.g., missing spec link, unclear base branch) before proceeding rather than guessing silently.

sw_001:n5.prompt:
You are helping me set up and run the AI code review pass (step sw_001:n5) in our 'spec to deploy' feature-shipping process, using {{vendor}} as the ai-code-review tool. If you don't already know it, ask me for: (1) my repo(s) or org name(s), (2) whether {{vendor}} is already installed/connected, and (3) the current feature branch or PR number to review.

Actions to take:
1. If {{vendor}} is not yet set up, walk through onboarding: connect our org and repo(s) so it can index the full codebase (not just diffs), and enable it as a GitHub/GitLab app so it can post native inline review comments on pull requests. If a CLI is available, use the equivalent of 'greptile onboard' to connect the org and repo and enable review.
2. Confirm the app has access to all relevant repos, including any spanning a monorepo or multiple services touched by this feature.
3. Trigger a review of the current feature branch's diff — via the CLI equivalent of 'greptile review' if available, or by opening/updating the PR so the app auto-reviews it.
4. Verify the review returns within minutes and includes: inline comments tied to specific lines, severity labels, deduplicated feedback (not repeating prior comments on re-review), and coverage of whole-repo context (call sites, related modules, conventions) — not just the changed hunks.
5. Confirm it flags both functional bugs (logic errors, race conditions, edge cases) and security issues (injection risks, leaked secrets, insecure patterns).
6. If new commits are pushed, confirm an incremental re-review runs and tracks resolved vs. outstanding comments.

Done looks like: {{vendor}} is connected and reviewing this PR with inline comments, severity levels, and low duplicate noise, covering both bugs and security issues.

Report back: setup status, the PR link, a summary of key findings by severity, and any unresolved comments needing developer or reviewer attention.

sw_001:n6.prompt:
You are helping me prepare a pull request for human review and approval before it merges into production. This is a policy-gate step: you must assemble everything a human reviewer needs, but you must NOT approve, merge, or submit the PR yourself.

First, ask me for anything missing: the repository name/URL, the PR number or branch, and any relevant spec/ticket link for the feature being shipped.

Then, using your configured credentials, do the following:
1. Fetch the PR's diff, description, and current status (open/draft, CI checks passing/failing, existing review comments).
2. Confirm the PR links to its originating spec/ticket; if missing, flag this clearly.
3. Summarize the change in plain language: what it does, files/modules touched, risk areas (e.g., migrations, auth, external calls), and test coverage added or modified.
4. Check that CI status checks and any required AI code review have completed and report their results (pass/fail, key findings).
5. Draft a concise review summary comment for the human reviewer, highlighting anything that needs their judgment (edge cases, security implications, backward compatibility, rollout risk).
6. Compile a short checklist: spec linked, tests present, CI green, AI review addressed, no unresolved comments.

Do not click approve, request changes, merge, or leave the summary as an actual PR comment unless I explicitly ask you to post it as a draft comment for me to review first. Do not resolve review threads or dismiss reviews.

When finished, report back: the PR link, your plain-language summary, CI/AI review status, the checklist with pass/fail marks, and the drafted reviewer-facing comment text. Then stop for human sign-off — I will personally review the code and checklist and decide whether to approve and merge.

sw_001:n7.prompt:
You are helping me merge and deploy an approved pull request through {{vendor}} (our code-hosting platform) as the final step of our ship-a-feature workflow. Approval requirement: a human must explicitly approve before changes are applied — do not merge or trigger deployment yourself without that sign-off.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already known: the repository name/URL, the PR number or branch, the target branch, and the CI/CD pipeline or workflow name that handles deployment.

Then, using your configured credentials to access {{vendor}}:
1. Open the specified pull request and confirm all required merge checks (status checks, required reviews, branch protection rules) are satisfied.
2. Summarize the PR's current state: check results, reviewer approvals, and any unresolved comments or conflicts.
3. Prepare a clear merge/deploy readiness report listing what passed, what's outstanding, and the exact merge action that would be taken (e.g., merge commit, squash, rebase) so a human can review it.
4. If everything required is green and a human has explicitly approved proceeding, you may perform the merge via {{vendor}}'s pull/merge request workflow, then monitor the CI/CD pipeline as it deploys the change, reporting build and deployment status as it progresses.
5. If anything is missing — a failing check, missing approval, or unclear deployment target — stop and flag it instead of proceeding.

If explicit human approval to merge has not yet been given, prepare everything above and then stop for human sign-off; do not merge or deploy on my behalf.

Done looks like: the PR is merged, the deployment pipeline has run successfully (or is actively running with status visible), and the feature is verifiable in production. Report back with the merge outcome, pipeline/build status, deployment URL or environment confirmation, and any warnings encountered.

sw_001:n8.prompt:
You are helping me verify that a feature I just deployed is healthy in production, using {{vendor}} as my error-tracking platform. Use your configured credentials for {{vendor}} and my issue tracker.

Ask me for these if you don't already have them:
- The {{vendor}} project(s) and environment name for production
- The release identifier or commit SHA that was just deployed, plus the deploy time
- The PR or ticket link for the feature, so you can tie findings back to it
- My issue tracker project for filing bugs

Steps:
1. Confirm {{vendor}} knows about this release. If no deploy or release record exists for it, tell me, and offer to record the deploy so errors are associated with the right release and commits.
2. Query production events since the deploy time, filtered by environment and release. Compare against the previous release's baseline for the same time window.
3. List issues first seen in this release, and any previously resolved issues that regressed (reopened) in this release. For each, pull the stack trace, event count, affected users, and the suspect commit if {{vendor}} shows one.
4. Triage. Decide whether each issue is caused by this feature, is pre-existing noise, or is a duplicate that was grouped incorrectly. Do not resolve, ignore, or snooze anything without checking with me first.
5. For real bugs linked to this feature, draft tracker tickets with the title, stack trace summary, release, suspect commit, and a link to the {{vendor}} issue. File them once I confirm.

Done looks like a clear verdict: "healthy", "healthy with minor issues", or "regressed, consider rollback".

Report back with:
- The verdict and the time window you checked
- A table of new and regressed issues, with your triage call and evidence for each
- Links to any tickets filed
- Anything you couldn't verify, such as a missing release tagging setup
